pitfalls: Do not declare a kind to change the picture — kinds never alter routing or layout; they set defaults and a lint axis.
Do not confuse strictness with validation: strict governs vocabulary membership only and never relaxes profile or geometry checks.
lessons.limits: Registered kinds are ddn-native, flowchart, the c4 and uml families, chart-bar/chart-line, ladder and patent-figure; an unknown kind is DDN-VP01, strictness without a kind is DDN-VP02. lessons.title: Patent and legal figures — numerals, refs and mono print
lessons.what: kind: patent-figure attaches the patent.legal@1 conventions: a boxed reference numeral under each element header, ref: anchors in prose that render as the target's numeral, and black-and-white page chrome with FIG. numbering.
lessons.why: Legal figures live by their numerals: the specification text references "valve 106", and a numeral that drifts from its element invalidates the page. Anchors computed at render time cannot drift.
lessons.when: Patent drawings, legal exhibits and any filing that must survive black-and-white reproduction with numbered parts.
read: Each element declares numeral: and wears it in a boxed field row; duplicates in one view fail DDN-VP06, out-of-range values DDN-VP05.
The note's ref:actuate renders as 106 — renumber the element and every anchor follows automatically.
The portrait page carries the header date, a single border and the FIG. $figure footer; the same model renders content-sized in the variant.
A decision branch without a label is warned (DDN-VP07) under this profile — examiners require every branch labelled.
inputs: The figure's elements and their numerals
The narration prose that references them
The page size and minimum text the filing office expects
pitfalls: Keep a ref: anchor and its target in the same data block — anchors resolve within the declaring block, and a cross-block anchor fails DDN-MK05.
Do not hand-type numerals into prose where an anchor exists; typed numbers drift, anchors do not.

lessons.title: Text fit — wrap, grow, shrink and honest overflow
lessons.what: How boxes adapt to their text: wrap fixes the width and grows downward, grow expands both axes to declared bounds, and shrink steps the font down to a floor.
lessons.why: Hand-tuning box sizes against text that keeps changing is the chore text_fit removes — with bounds and diagnostics so adaptation stays honest instead of silently clipping.
lessons.when: Long labels, generated text, multilingual content — anywhere text length is not under the author's full control.
read: The renderer measures, resizes and re-lays-out in at most two passes; whatever still overflows after that is a residual overflow and is reported.
Residual overflow fires DDN-LW07 (wrap/grow) or DDN-LW08 (shrink at its floor) at render time, naming the element, the overflow and the remedy — check stays clean because it never measures.

Under the default layout { quality: error } a residual overflow refuses the render; the variant declares quality: warn, so it renders with the text clipped at the box edge and a visible ellipsis — never invisible text.
size: content artboards grow with the post-fit bounds, so wrap/grow results are always fully visible — and --content-size forces that for one render without editing the source.
inputs: The text and how much it may vary
pitfalls: Do not set max_height without reading DDN-LW07 as a design signal — split the content or raise the bound; clipping is a last resort, not a layout style.
Do not rely on estimated metrics for filings: font_pin records the measurement environment so the same source renders byte-identically anywhere (pin files load through the CLI and the host API).
lessons.limits: Bounds are 40–4000 px and min_font 6–64 px (never above the base font); violations are DDN-TF02/TF03. Text fit changes geometry only — model fingerprints, endpoints and relation identities are unchanged.
lessons.editTask: Lengthen the summary note, apply, and watch the box grow within its bounds; then open the overflow variant to meet the ellipsis and DDN-LW07.

lessons.title: Parameterized fragments — one template, many instances
lessons.what: A fragment declares 1-8 parameters (fragment staged(name, table) {…}) and each use: binds them positionally, stamping out declarations as if handwritten; definitions may also apply other definitions (nested use:).
lessons.why: A pipeline of identical stages is one template, not five copies to keep in sync: rename the stage kind or add a field once and every instance follows — with identities exactly as if you had typed each stage out.
lessons.when: Repeated sub-models (stages, tiers, mirrored pairs), template libraries shared across files, any place a copy-paste block keeps drifting.
read: staged(name, table) stamps a service card and its flow to the audit trail; pipeline(first, second) applies it twice (nested use:) and chains the stages — ingest and reconcile render like any handwritten card.

Substitution is token-level: a declaration id, a whole @reference, a whole property value, or ${name} inside a string. name_out would be one token — identifiers never interpolate inside, so kebab rules always hold.

The expansion is IR-identical to the handwritten model: equivalence is gated by fixtures, and inspectors treat expanded content as derived/read-only — edit the use: site (local override) or the fragment (all instances).
Cycles between definitions are DDN-FG04 and nesting past 8 levels is DDN-FG05; arity, unknown ${…}, and bad identifier args are DDN-FG01/FG02/FG03.
inputs: The repeated shape and what varies per instance
Parameter names and their positions (id, reference, value, string)
pitfalls: Do not expect name_out-style identifier interpolation — put the varying part in a whole id token or a ${…} string.
Do not edit an expanded instance hoping to change the template — expansions are derived; edit the fragment or override at the use: site.
lessons.limits: Arguments bind positionally (DDN-FG01); an argument that cannot serve its position is DDN-FG03. Below ddn "0.6" parameters/arguments are DDN-V04 and nested use: stays DDN-E017.

lessons.title: Diff views — before/after in one picture
lessons.what: A view with diff: [@v1, @v2] renders the union of both views’ visible models with per-member states: added, removed, changed and unchanged.
lessons.why: Reviewing a change means seeing it, not reconstructing it from two files: one picture shows what appeared, what vanished and what moved — generated from the model, never hand-drawn.
lessons.when: Migration plans, review packets, change proposals, before/after teaching material — anywhere two revisions of a model need one shared reading.
read: Members match by local source id: before.worker and after.worker are the same element, so it paints changed (amber, dotted, ~) — it gained a retries field; legacy is removed (red, dashed, struck, −); ingest is added (green, solid, +); store is unchanged and gets no overlay.
Relations carry their own states: r1 is removed, r3 is added, r2 is unchanged — a relation’s state reflects its own record, so an endpoint’s change shows on the element, not the edge.
The diff key beside the title names the operands and the three state channels; under neutral or mono_print the colours drop out and the dash, strike and token channels keep the states readable.
The union is laid out fresh — the operands’ geometry is ignored, so a removed element appears where the union places it among its former neighbours.

Which members should correlate (shared local ids)
The diff view’s own layout and publication
pitfalls: Do not rely on uid: to correlate revisions — uids are workspace-unique by construction; the shared local source id is the identity claim.
Do not diff a view against itself or a diff of a diff (DDN-DF03) — operands are ordinary views.
lessons.limits: diff and data: are mutually exclusive (DDN-DF01); an operand with duplicate local ids is DDN-DF04 (narrow with select/exclude). Below ddn "0.6" any diff is DDN-V04.

lessons.why: "This path must not exist" and "this box is a draft" are design facts; keeping them in the model means they export, diff and render under every theme — instead of living in someone's slide notes.

read: The forbidden relation is struck and barred — under mono_print the treatment is hatch and dash, never colour alone, so the signal survives any theme.

lessons.title: CLI power tools — verbs, diagnostics JSON and publish
lessons.what: The command-line surface beyond check and render: the verbs legality query, machine-readable diagnostics, one-off render overrides, publication-set publishing and the strict-print gate.
lessons.why: Scripts and CI need answers, not pictures: which verb may connect these kinds, which diagnostics fired and where, and whether the page survives print rules — all without opening a tool.
lessons.when: Authoring assistance (verbs), CI gates (--diagnostics json, --strict-print), documentation pipelines (publish) and quick previews (--content-size).
read: cli.js verbs --from service --to database lists the verbs whose registered endpoint contract admits the pair (add --json for the machine form); an unknown kind fails DDN-WS01, and an empty list means no legal verb — still exit 0.
check --diagnostics json emits the stable shape {code, severity, file, line, view, message}; file is the workspace-relative POSIX path and line is 1-based, so CI can deep-link any finding.

The gate the CI must enforce

Contacts in series are AND; contacts stacked on parallel tracks are OR.
One rung drives exactly one coil — the validator enforces it.
pitfalls: A rung with two coils is an error, not a design.
Branches come from the wiring topology — you do not declare them.
lessons.limits: Common-practice ladder rendering and validation; no PLC compilation, execution or IEC XML interchange.

lessons.title: Typed decision table — first match
lessons.what: A typed decision table evaluated in first-match order: the first row whose conditions all match produces the outcome.
lessons.why: Expose rule order as a deliberate design decision instead of an accident of presentation.
lessons.when: Bounded business rules where precedence must be reviewable line by line.
read: Read rows top-down: the first fully-matching row wins.
Type domains on each input gate what a row may claim.
inputs: The input fields and their domains
The rule rows in priority order
pitfalls: Row order is normative here — reordering rows changes outcomes.
A gap in the domain is a silent fall-through, not a default row.
lessons.limits: Bounded decision-table evaluation against one input record; no arbitrary rule-language execution.
lessons.editTask: Evaluate the table against one input record with evaluateDecision, then swap two rows and evaluate again — the outcome difference is the lesson.
